one_liner: Parameter-free FIFO-plus-moving-hand eviction policy that beats LRU on miss ratio and multi-thread throughput for web caches.
what_it_does: SIEVE is a cache eviction algorithm (NSDI'24) meant to replace LRU in web, CDN and key-value caches. It uses one FIFO queue, one visited bit per object and a 'hand' pointer. The catalogued repo, libCacheSim, is a C cache simulator in which SIEVE is one policy among more than 30: you run `cachesim <trace> <type> sieve <size>` or call `Sieve_init()` behind the generic `cache->get(cache, req)` API. It stores no values and is not a production cache. The throughput numbers come from a separate CacheLib fork with an MMSieve container, and production use usually means adding 12-21 lines to an existing linked-list LRU, as the authors did for groupcache, lru-rs, mnemonist and lru-dict, or taking one of the ports listed on sievecache.com.
how_it_is_fast: A hit only sets the object's visited bit. Nothing moves in the queue, so the hit path takes no list lock. In the CacheLib prototype a hit is a flag write, inserts use a CAS on the list head, and only eviction and removal take a folly::DistributedMutex. On a miss the hand walks from the tail toward the head, clearing visited bits and evicting the first unvisited object; objects that survive keep their position instead of being reinserted at the head as in CLOCK/FIFO-Reinsertion. The paper calls the result 'lazy promotion' plus 'quick demotion': new objects sit between the head and the hand and get examined soon after insertion, so one-hit wonders leave quickly, and in the simulator SIEVE ran up to 40% fewer instructions per request than LRU.
when_to_use: Object, CDN or key-value caches with skewed (Zipf/power-law) popularity and few scans. This is the paper's domain: 1559 traces from Twitter, Meta, Wikimedia, Tencent and two CDNs, where SIEVE had the lowest miss ratio of 10 algorithms on more than 45% of traces.
Swapping out a doubly-linked-list LRU in an in-process cache when you want no tuning parameters and a change of about 20 lines (12-21 lines in the paper's four library ports).

Multi-threaded caches where LRU's move-to-head on every hit causes lock contention. The CacheLib prototype was 16% faster than CacheLib's optimized LRU at 1 thread and more than 2x faster at 16 threads on the Meta KV trace.
Mid-to-large caches, around 10% of the trace footprint, where the gains are largest: a mean 21% lower miss ratio than FIFO on the CDN1 dataset, against 15% for CLOCK.
As a building block that replaces the LRU queue inside ARC, TwoQ or LeCaR. ARC-SIEVE cut ARC's miss ratio by a mean of 3.7% (up to 62.5%) over the 1559 traces.
when_not_to_use: Block, page or file caches with scans or loops, such as database buffer pools or backup reads. The paper's §7 says SIEVE is not scan-resistant (it has no ghost queue) and sometimes has a higher miss ratio than LRU on block workloads. A co-author wrote on HN that when the hand sits near the head it evicts new objects in an MRU-like way and 'may not be robust'.

Very small caches (0.1% of footprint): TwoQ and LHD sometimes beat it because new objects are evicted before they can show popularity. On two Wiki CDN traces, LRB beat it on byte miss ratio at 1-2% cache sizes.

Workloads whose popular set changes abruptly. When the paper switched between two Zipf workloads, SIEVE had a larger transient miss-ratio spike than LRU or ARC because the hand has to travel back to the tail before old objects can go.

When you need a ready-made C/C++ cache library. libCacheSim is a simulator, the CacheLib prototype is a research fork last pushed in December 2023, and SIEVE is not in upstream facebook/CacheLib (its tree has no MMSieve).

Ring-buffer or log-structured stores. SIEVE evicts from the middle of the queue, so it needs a linked list (17 B of per-object metadata in the paper's Table 3), and a co-author called circular-buffer or log-structured implementations 'not trivial'.

integration.form: source-drop (the algorithm). In the catalogued repo, Sieve.c is one policy inside libCacheSim, a CMake/Ninja-built C library and cachesim binary, and it holds no values. The CacheLib prototype is a full CacheLib fork. Third-party ports include kassane/sieve-cache-cpp (header-only, C++17, MIT).
integration.dependencies: The algorithm has none. libCacheSim needs glib-2.0 and zstd (zstd trace support is on by default); tcmalloc is optional. The CacheLib prototype needs CacheLib's full dependency set (folly, etc.), installed through contrib/build.sh.
integration.min_toolchain: libCacheSim: CMake 3.12+ with CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 for its C++ parts; the minimum C standard and compiler versions are not documented. CacheLib prototype: CacheLib's 2023 build script, tested on CentOS 8, Ubuntu 18.04 and Debian 10. kassane/sieve-cache-cpp: C++17 (uses std::pmr).
integration.platforms: The algorithm runs anywhere. libCacheSim documents installation on Ubuntu and macOS; the Node binding ships a prebuilt binary for Linux x64 only; Windows is not documented. The throughput results were measured on x86-64 (Xeon Gold 6142).
integration.thread_safety: libCacheSim: Sieve.c takes no locks and each cache_t is single-threaded; the simulator parallelizes across independent cache instances and sizes. CacheLib prototype: hits set an access flag without the container lock, head inserts are lock-free (CAS), and eviction and removal hold a folly::DistributedMutex. kassane/sieve-cache-cpp has no locking.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: SIEVE replaces LRU's hit and evict logic inside an existing linked-list cache with about 12-21 lines, and the get/put API stays the same. libCacheSim's Sieve.c itself is a simulator policy, not a cache you can store data in.

gotchas: Because eviction happens in the middle of the queue, deleting an object the hand points at must move the hand to its neighbour (libCacheSim's Sieve_remove_obj sets hand = prev). Ports that skip this leave a dangling hand. Eviction is also worst-case O(N) when most objects have their visited bit set.

The CacheLib prototype is research-grade code. SieveList::getEvictionCandidate printf's and abort()s after more than two full sweeps, and unlink() calls try_lock() then abort() as its lock-held check. A null-tail race between lock-free linkAtHead and unlink was reported and fixed only in the sibling AtomicDList (PR #1, Dec 2023); SieveList still inserts at the head lock-free.

Third-party ports vary in quality. kassane/sieve-cache-cpp's get() allocates and returns a shared_ptr copy of the value on every hit, its constructor calls std::pmr::set_default_resource (a process-wide side effect), and it has no mutex.

Most of the headline miss-ratio results ignore object size (the paper assumes slab-style caches). Byte miss ratio is shown only for the CDN traces, and the paper's mean ARC-over-LRU reduction appears as both 6.7% and 6.3%.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick SIEVE over LHD or W-TinyLFU/Caffeine when you are patching an existing C/C++ linked-list LRU for web or KV traffic and want a parameter-free change of about 20 lines with a lock-free hit path. LHD has tuning parameters and far more code (192/81/64 lines for hit/evict/insert against SIEVE's 4/9/3) but wins at very small caches. Caffeine is a complete concurrent JVM library, and W-TinyLFU is the safer choice when scans or an unknown workload mix are likely.
verified_claims_summary: Throughput: a CacheLib-based C++ prototype (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23) ran on a CloudLab c6420 (dual Xeon Gold 6142 @ 2.6 GHz, 384 GB DDR4, turbo off, threads pinned to one NUMA node; compiler and flags not stated). It replayed Meta and Twitter KV traces with a cache of 4 GB × threads (miss ratios 7% and 2%), and SIEVE beat CacheLib's optimized LRU by 16% (TwoQ by 17%) at 1 thread and more than 2x at 16 threads on the Meta trace. Miss ratio was measured separately in the libCacheSim simulator over 1559 traces: a mean 21% lower than FIFO on CDN1 at the large cache size, and up to 63.2% (mean 1.5%) lower than ARC.
status_note: libCacheSim is actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-26, Apache-2.0, 347 stars), but Sieve.c has had only cosmetic edits since January 2024, and the CacheLib throughput prototype (Apache-2.0, 11 stars) has not been pushed since 2023-12-13. The algorithm is small enough to copy into your own cache, which is how the listed adopters (TiDB, Ceph, DragonFly, PostgREST, DNSCrypt-proxy, Immudb and others) use it.
